blocks.text: This is a flower. In winter it waits under the ground. The sun stays low. The days are short and cold. Then spring comes. The days get long. The sun feels warm. The rain soaks the dirt. blocks.prompt: The Flower and the Bee
blocks.text: A flower is not just pretty. It is how a plant makes seeds. Look in the middle of a flower. There is a sweet drink there called nectar. A bee wants that nectar. When the bee climbs in, yellow dust sticks to her fuzzy legs. That dust is pollen. The bee flies to the next flower. Some pollen rubs off. Now that flower can make seeds. The bright petals are a sign. They tell the bee where to land. The smell helps too. Bees can smell a flower from far away.

blocks.prompt: Why Flowers Wait for Spring
blocks.text: A flower has one job. It has to make seeds, and it has to do it at the right time. Open too early and a frost will kill the buds. Open too late and winter will arrive before the seeds are ready. So a plant has to read the weather. It cannot see a calendar, but it can feel two things: light and cold. Under the ground, a bulb waits out the winter. It is not sleeping. It is counting. It keeps track of how long the cold lasts. A tulip that never gets a cold winter will often refuse to bloom at all. When spring comes, the sun climbs higher and the days stretch out. The soil warms. The plant adds up the light and the warmth, and when the total is high enough, it starts to build a bud. The flower opens. Petals spread. Nectar fills the middle. And the bees, who have been waiting through the same winter, arrive right on time. The plant and the bee are reading the same weather.

notes: Photoperiodism: timing by the length of the dark

blocks.prompt: The Plant That Counts the Dark
blocks.text: You would think a plant waits for spring by feeling the warmth. Warmth is part of it. But warmth is a liar. A mild week in February can feel exactly like April, and a plant that trusted it would open its buds straight into the next frost. So plants measure something that cannot be faked: the length of the night. In 1920, two scientists named Wightman Garner and Harry Allard were studying a tobacco plant that grew huge and green but would not flower out in the summer field. They tried moving it into a dark shed for part of each day. It bloomed. The plant did not want more light. It wanted more darkness. Their discovery is called photoperiodism. Plants track the hours of unbroken dark, and different plants need different amounts. Chrysanthemums flower once nights grow long, which is why you see them in fall. Spinach flowers when nights grow short. Here is the strange part. If you interrupt a long night with a single flash of light, some plants act as though the night never happened, and they will not flower. Their count starts over from zero. Growers use this on purpose. They switch lamps on in the middle of the night, or leave them off, to bring a crop of flowers into bloom for a holiday, weeks before the weather outside says so.

notes: The leaves do the measuring, not the flower

Vernalization: cold releases a brake on flowering

blocks.prompt: Reading the Weather Without Eyes
blocks.text: A plant has no eyes, no brain, and no calendar. It still manages to open its flowers within a few days of the same date every year. How it does that is one of the neatest pieces of engineering in the natural world. Start with the sensor. The measuring is not done by the flower. It is done by the leaves. Leaves carry a pigment called phytochrome, which comes in two forms that flip back and forth. Red daylight flips it into its active form. Through a long dark night, it slowly relaxes back again. The plant is not counting hours the way a clock does. It is reading how far that pigment has drifted by dawn, and the amount of drift is a measure of how long the night was. Then the message has to travel. The leaf senses the season, but the flower gets built at the tip of a shoot, sometimes far away. For decades nobody could find the messenger. A Russian scientist named Mikhail Chailakhyan argued in 1937 that some signal must move from leaf to shoot, and he gave it a name before anyone had ever seen it: florigen. It took about seventy years to catch. Florigen turned out to be a protein, made in the leaf and pushed up through the plant's plumbing to the growing tip, where it switches on the genes that build a flower. There is a second lock on the door. Many plants will not flower at all until they have lived through a real winter. Cold does not encourage them. Cold removes a brake. All through the freezing weeks, a gene that had been blocking flowering is quietly switched off, one cold day at a time, and it stays off through the spring. Botanists call this vernalization. It is why tulip bulbs sit in a refrigerator at the garden shop, and why some fruit trees planted in warm climates simply never bloom. They are still waiting for a winter that never comes. Put the pieces together and a flower is a weather instrument. It measures the dark, remembers the cold, adds up the warmth, and then commits. And once the bud opens, there is no taking it back.

notes: Kyoto bloom dates run from the year 812
The longest record of a natural event we have

Compiled by researcher Yasuyuki Aono
2021: earliest full bloom in over 1,200 years
Cherry trees count cold first, then add up warmth

blocks.prompt: The Longest Weather Record on Earth Is Written in Flowers
blocks.text: There is a spreadsheet kept at a university in Japan with a column of dates in it that begins in the year 812. It is the longest record of a repeating natural event that humans have ever assembled, and it is not a record of floods, harvests, or storms. It is a list of the days on which the cherry trees of Kyoto reached full bloom. Nobody set out to build it. For more than a thousand years, Japanese courtiers, monks, and officials wrote down when they held their blossom parties, because the blossom mattered to them. They noted it in diaries and poems and temple chronicles, the way you might note a birthday. A researcher named Yasuyuki Aono spent years reading those documents and pulling the dates out of them. The result is an accidental climate archive, assembled by people who were only trying to remember a good afternoon. To understand why those dates are useful, you have to know what a cherry tree is actually doing. A flowering tree does not wake up because the weather is nice. It runs a two-stage program. Through the winter, it counts cold. A gene that blocks flowering is switched off, one cold week at a time, and only when enough chill has been banked does the tree unlock. That stage is called vernalization. Then, in spring, the tree begins adding up warmth. When the running total crosses a threshold, the buds open, and the tree has no say in the matter. It cannot be optimistic or cautious. It is a thermometer that reports its reading by blooming. This is what makes the Kyoto record valuable. A diary entry from 1409 is not an opinion about the weather. It is a measurement of that spring, taken by a tree, written down by a person who had no idea he was taking one. Read the column from top to bottom and a shape appears. For most of a millennium the dates wobble around the middle of April, drifting a few days either way as cold centuries and mild ones came and went. Then, across roughly the last hundred and fifty years, the wobble stops being a wobble and starts being a slope. The dates walk steadily earlier. In 2021 the Kyoto cherries reached full bloom on March 26, the earliest date in more than 1,200 years of records. The honest reading of that slope has two parts, and they are worth separating. Kyoto is now a large city, and cities run warmer than the countryside around them, because concrete and asphalt hold the day's heat and release it at night. Some of the shift belongs to the city itself. But rural Japanese trees are moving earlier too, and so are the shorter flowering records kept in Europe and North America. The city explains part of the slope. It does not explain all of it. There is one more turn to this. Cherry trees need their winter. If warm winters shorten the cold-counting stage, a tree can arrive at spring without ever having finished the first half of its program, and the bloom comes late, thin, or ragged instead of early. Warmer does not simply mean sooner. Past a certain point it means worse. The people who kept these records were not scientists. They were writing about a party under the trees. But they were careful, they were consistent, and they kept it up for twelve hundred years, which is the whole trick of a good measurement. Somebody wrote down the day the flowers opened, and then somebody else did it the next year, and nobody stopped. The cherry trees have been reporting the temperature of Japan since before England had a Norman king, and it took us until now to read the report.
